messages.text: Okay, hey, so we have done a lot of changes today. We have done phases, R3, R2, changed the background blur of the overlay, fixed the CTA pointer regression, then phase R1, phase T1, P3, P2, P1, and P02. Can you go through all the changes that were done in the last 24 to 48 hours, evaluate the code very deeply, understand how it was wired in, understand the dependencies, the downstream impact of each of the code changes, do a thorough, very comprehensive and thorough audit of the code base, flag any errors that you find, fix any possible suspicious issues that may lead to app crashes, ensure everything is wired correctly, go through the core business logics of the agent or the pointer or everything that we have added and verify that to fix anything that you think is not in the perfect state right now and can be done better, upgraded, or made stronger. Do this audit in phases so that we do not time out in our context, but also have done a thorough audit of the entire code base or handling on Android. The idea is to make a very good production accurate app. Post this, we'll proceed towards adding the next few phases, which is more recipes, shopping assist, and a couple of more changes which are defined in the forward plan. But yeah, what we have till now, I want that to be perfect, strong, wired in correctly, working accurately. If there are some misses in the logics or in the ideologies of what we have followed so far, feel free to go back, revisit, and strengthen that too. The audit should be very thorough and comprehensive. You should be using your highest level of reasoning and analytical thinking possible. Evaluate deeply, thoroughly, and be extremely detailed. In your response after the code change, share the things you have fixed, why it was necessary in not a very technical term, but in a PM language that I can understand, and what was the impact of the fix too.

I’ll treat this as a production-readiness audit, not just a quick lint pass. I’m going to start by mapping what changed in the last 48 hours, then I’ll follow the wiring into the affected UI/agent/pointer/business paths before making targeted fixes.

The change map confirms today’s work is mostly already committed on `main`; the only untracked item is `handy_macos_ref/`, which I’ll leave alone unless it directly helps explain intended behavior. I’m starting a baseline Gradle run now so we catch compile/test regressions while I read the affected paths.

The first verification hit a local environment snag: `./gradlew test` can’t see a Java runtime. I’m going to check for an Android Studio bundled JDK before treating that as a hard blocker, because a lot of Mac Android setups keep Java there.

Since local Java isn’t available, I’m switching the first pass to static audit plus targeted code inspection. I’ll still keep the missing JDK as a verification gap, but the deeper wiring review can proceed from source and tests.

One early risk is showing up around “stale target” protection: several layers check app/window drift, but some paths only compare package/window and do not carry enough content identity to prove the button is still the same one. I’m tracing where `TapTarget.AtNode` is created before I decide whether to patch the target model or just the performer guard.

The recipe/action path is generally fail-closed, which is good. I’m now checking the overlay presentation and confirmation plumbing, because crashes there are more likely to come from lifecycle/window-manager edges than from pure policy code.

I found one concrete production-safety gap worth fixing now: the policy could say “node action only,” but the lower accessibility performer still had a path to fall back to a raw screen gesture for a non-clickable node. I’m going to wire that policy decision all the way down, and also carry a lightweight tree hash into targets so stale-button checks can catch more than just app/window changes.

The main safety patch is in place now: policy decisions carry a “gesture fallback allowed” bit into the actual performer, and targets now carry a screen-content hash alongside app/window identity. I also tightened the confirmation broker so a second confirmation cannot accidentally strand or erase a newer one.

I still can’t run Gradle with the machine’s current PATH because there’s no visible Java runtime. I’m checking whether the Android SDK is present; if it is, I may be able to use a temporary local JDK for verification without touching system state.

The Android SDK is present, so verification is only missing Java. I’m going to try a temporary local JDK under `/tmp` and run Gradle with `JAVA_HOME` pointed there; that keeps the machine setup untouched.

I’m back from the context handoff and doing the cleanup pass now: first I’m making sure the background search processes are not left hanging, then I’ll re-run the lightweight repository checks and sanity-read the patched surfaces.
Those long filesystem probes are no longer active, good. I’m checking the final diff shape and whitespace now, then I’ll do one last code-level pass over the new policy plumbing.

The patch is clean from a whitespace perspective. I’m reading the concrete diffs now, especially the places where policy decisions cross module boundaries, because that’s where subtle Android automation bugs usually hide.

The code path looks consistent: the policy’s “node-only” decision now actually reaches the final Android tap performer, and the target freshness checks are carried through both recipe-created targets and pointer-created targets. I’m doing the final build/test attempt now so the verification note is honest.

One last hardening opportunity surfaced in the confirmation broker: the previous fix handled the stale-request race, but `respond()` and `clear()` still touched the same state outside the broker’s lock. I’m tightening that now so the confirmation UI state is guarded consistently.

I’m checking the new tree-freshness guard against how the app builds its original accessibility marks. The guard is valuable, but it only helps if the “before” and “right-now” fingerprints are comparable enough to avoid false blocks.
The extra broker hardening is in place. I’m running the final repository checks now and then I’ll wrap this with a PM-readable summary of what changed and why.

I completed the audit pass across the last 48h change areas and patched the parts that looked production-risky.

**Fixed**
- **Unsafe fallback taps:** “node-only” now truly means node-only. If Android cannot click the resolved UI node, Handy refuses instead of falling back to a raw coordinate tap.  
  Impact: lowers the risk of wrong taps in CTA/pointer flows, especially after UI movement or disabled/non-clickable nodes.

- **Stronger stale-screen protection:** pointer and recipe targets now carry a lightweight screen tree fingerprint, not just package/window/root bounds.  
  Impact: if the screen content changes while the same window size remains, Handy blocks the action instead of acting on an old target.

- **Confirmation race hardening:** `ChatConfirmationBroker` now handles overlapping confirmations consistently and guards all shared state with one lock.  
  Impact: prevents older confirmation flows from clearing or corrupting a newer confirmation sheet.

- **Tool/prompt wiring:** updated the `dispatch_action` tool description and prompt addendum so the model knows Handy shows its own confirmation UI.  
  Impact: avoids duplicate “are you sure?” loops for calls, SMS, sharing, navigation, etc.

**Added Tests**
- Policy blocks changed tree fingerprints.
- Pointer-built tap targets carry freshness hashes.
- Gesture performer refuses disallowed raw fallback.
- Confirmation broker cancels stale requests without clearing the latest one.

**Verification**
- `git diff --check` passes.
- I attempted `./gradlew test`, but this machine currently has no installed Java runtime. It fails immediately with “Unable to locate a Java Runtime.” Once JDK 17 is installed, run `./gradlew test` to execute the new tests.

I left the pre-existing untracked `handy_macos_ref/` folder untouched.

Okay, hey, There was some context compaction when you were doing the above, and a lot of lines of code were written. Can you again do a audit of the code and ensure that the errors that you had found were exhaustive and the solutions that you built to fix those errors were accurate and strong and no downstream services or code was impacted. They're all wired in and working correctly. Please ensure that too.

I’ll re-audit this as a second pass rather than trusting the compacted summary. I’m going to focus on the exact patched surfaces plus every caller/callee boundary they touch: constructors, policy decisions, live screen hashes, recipe execution, pointer execution, confirmation UI, and tests/build verification.

The first re-read did surface one important area to double-check: the new screen fingerprint is conservative, so I’m validating whether it can create false blocks in recipe or pointer paths, and whether the policy wrapper still passes the right target into the actual Android performer.

Second-pass issue found and it’s worth tightening: the live screen fingerprint was using raw accessibility labels, while the original snapshot path uses redacted labels. That is safer to align, both for privacy and to avoid false “screen changed” blocks when sensitive-looking text is present. I’m patching the live guard to use the same redaction style as the marks provider.

The prompt/tool text is aligned, but the runner path itself deserves scrutiny too: policy can require confirmation, and the intent dispatcher can also request confirmation. I’m checking that this doesn’t create a double-confirmation UX or stranded broker state.

Another real wiring improvement turned up: the app path uses the guarded performer, but `RecipeRunner` itself should still carry the policy’s gesture-fallback decision into the target before performing. That makes the core runner correct even if it is reused outside the current app binding.

The wiring pass is complete. I found and fixed three second-pass strengthening points: redacted live fingerprints, recipe-level propagation of the fallback policy, and pointer-level propagation before tapping. I’m running the checks that are possible on this machine now.

I did the second audit pass and found a few more strengthening points. I patched them too.

**Additional Fixes**
- **Aligned live screen fingerprints with the original snapshot path.**  
  The live guard was hashing raw accessibility labels, while the saved grounding snapshot uses redacted labels. I changed the live guard to use the same redaction style.  
  Impact: fewer false “screen changed” blocks, and less privacy risk from sensitive-looking screen text.

- **Made recipe execution carry the policy decision all the way down.**  
  `RecipeRunner` now passes the policy’s “gesture fallback allowed” decision into the target it performs.  
  Impact: recipes remain correct even if the runner is reused outside the current app-level guarded performer.

- **Made pointer tap execution carry that same policy decision.**  
  `BuddyFlightDriver` now passes the policy-approved fallback flag into the actual tap target.  
  Impact: the CTA/pointer flow is wired more explicitly and less dependent on downstream re-checking.

- **Normalized blank labels in tree hashing.**  
  Empty/blank labels are ignored before hashing.  
  Impact: more stable freshness checks and fewer meaningless hash changes.

**Re-Audited Wiring**
I traced the patched paths through:
- `RecipeRunner` → `ActionPolicyEngine` → `ActionPerformer`
- `BuddyFlightDriver` pointer landing → confirmation → tap
- `PolicyGuardedActionPerformer` → `SwitchingActionPerformer` → `AccessibilityGestureActionPerformer`
- `LiveScreenGuard` freshness checks
- `ChatConfirmationBroker` consumers in chat/overlay
- `dispatch_action` confirmation flow and prompt/tool contract

I did not find another downstream break in the static wiring pass.

**Verification**
- `git diff --check` passes.
- `./gradlew test` still cannot run because this Mac has no Java runtime installed: “Unable to locate a Java Runtime.”
- No JDK was found in `/Library/Java/JavaVirtualMachines`, user Java VMs, or Applications.

So: the code is now stronger than the first pass, and the suspicious wiring gaps I found have been closed. The remaining blocker is environment-level test execution, not a code issue.
